 "sports": ["Track & Field"],
 "populations": ["Healthy Athletes", "Male Athletes", "Female Athletes", "Professional / Elite", "Youth / Adolescent", "Mixed / Unspecified"],
 "evidenceSummary": "Systematic review of 10 mostly cross-sectional studies (684 participants; 4,811 records screened) on lower-limb inter-limb asymmetry and sprinting performance in healthy, injury-free sprint athletes, with no meta-analysis because studies were few and heterogeneous. Most functional, morphological, kinematic and kinetic asymmetry measures were not significantly associated with sprint performance, with a few metric- and sex-specific associations in single studies. GRADE certainty was very low for every outcome.",
 "screeningLimitations": "Every association comes from a single study (k = 1 per outcome), all but one study were cross-sectional, and only 3 of 10 checked the reliability of their asymmetry measures. Training level was reported for only 162 participants (16 world class, 8 elite, 138 highly trained), and the largest cohort (Trivers et al., n = 288) had no training status reported.",
 "synthesisCaution": "Staff could read the mostly null results as proof that asymmetry never matters for sprinting, or the few significant single-study correlations as a reason to target it, when the certainty is very low and the design cannot show cause and effect.",
 "paper": {
  "year": 2026,
  "citation": "D'Hondt J, Chapelle L, Van Handenhoven J, Stalmans J, Aerenhouts D. The Relationship Between Inter-limb Asymmetry and Sprinting Performance in Sprint Athletes: A Systematic Review. Sports Med Open. 2026;12:146.",
  "doi": "10.1186/s40798-026-01082-1",
  "abstract": "Systematic review of 10 studies (from 4,811 screened records) on the association between lower-limb inter-limb asymmetry and sprinting performance in healthy, injury-free sprint athletes. Associations were limited overall, with task- and metric-specific links in individual studies, and the authors call the evidence mixed.",
  "tldr": "In sprinters, most measures of left-right asymmetry were not linked to sprint performance, and the few links came from single small studies rated very low certainty. Asymmetry on its own is not a strong reason to change a sprinter's training.",
  "methods": "PRISMA 2020 review (PROSPERO CRD420251140520) searching PubMed, Scopus, SPORTDiscus and Web of Science to 17 March 2026, plus citation tracking, for studies of lower-limb asymmetry and sprint performance (up to 400 m) in healthy, injury-free sprint athletes of any age and level. Quality was rated with a modified 10-item Downs and Black checklist (scores 6-8/10) and certainty with GRADE; results were synthesized narratively.",
  "findings": "Most asymmetry measures showed no significant association, including all kinetic measures in 64 highly trained sprinters (Nagahara et al.) and short-term changes in asymmetry over one month in 13 sprinters (Gleadhill et al.). Single small studies reported sex-specific kinematic links in 16 world-class sprinters (r = -0.86 in males, r = 0.81 in females), net ankle work asymmetry linked to 60 m velocity in 8 males (r = 0.90), and textile EMG asymmetry linked to 50 m time in 8 elite females (rs 0.36 to 0.59). In Jamaican cohorts, knee joint width and composite asymmetry had significant but very small associations with 90 m and 180 m velocity and IAAF scores (R2 0.02 to 0.05).",
  "limitations": "Asymmetry dimensions, equations, tasks, sex, age and training status varied widely, so the authors judged a meta-analysis inappropriate, and all outcomes were downgraded for risk of bias and imprecision to very low certainty. The text conflicts on the Trivers results: the results report knee joint width asymmetry as positively associated with 90 m velocity (beta 0.21 to 0.24), while the discussion says it was linked to lower velocities; the results also once refer to a 'systematic review with meta-analysis' although none was done.",
  "practicalImplications": "The authors conclude that reducing asymmetry does not need to be a central focus of sprint training for performance, given the inconsistent links. If asymmetry is measured, use the same task and metric over time and know the test's reliability, since most included studies did not.",
  "athleteDev": "Performance staff should not assume that reducing a between-limb difference will improve sprint speed, because no included study tested that. Interpret any asymmetry score against the specific test and metric used, because the few associations were task-, metric- and sex-specific.",
  "rtp": "Limited application to return to sport: the review included only healthy, injury-free athletes, so it cannot show whether asymmetry after injury affects sprint readiness or re-injury risk."
 },
 "verification": {
  "status": "CORRECTED",
  "changes": [
   "evidenceSummary: 'the evidence was rated mixed with GRADE' -> GRADE certainty was very low for every outcome ('The certainty of evidence across all outcomes was rated as very low'); added 684 participants and mostly cross-sectional design",
   "paper.findings: only the 60 m composite kinematic result -> added the null kinetic results in 64 sprinters, the single-study significant associations with their sample sizes (Bissas n = 16, Exell n = 8, Golas n = 8) and the very small Trivers effects ('R2 = 0.02 to 0.05')",
   "screeningLimitations: added k = 1 per outcome, one longitudinal study, reliability in 3 of 10, and that the largest cohort had no training status ('In one particular study, the training level was not specified')",
   "paper.limitations: added very low certainty and the Trivers direction conflict between results ('positively associated with mean velocity over 90 m') and discussion ('associated with poorer performance (i.e. lower mean velocities')",
   "populations: added Professional / Elite (16 world class, 8 elite) and Youth / Adolescent (Prvulovic, mean age 15.9, 18 females)",
   "paper.methods: added sprint distance scope, citation tracking, quality score range and narrative synthesis",
   "paper.practicalImplications: dropped 'standardised assessment before drawing practical conclusions' as advice -> consistent task, metric and known reliability, matching the review's reliability finding"
  ],
  "residualConcerns": "The direction of the Trivers knee-width finding cannot be settled from the text (positive beta with velocity in results, 'poorer performance' in the discussion). Sex counts (324 male, 265 female, 95 unreported) and the Trivers cohort sizes in Table 6 (288 and 163) do not reconcile cleanly, and one Trivers study scored IAAF results from 100 m to 800 m. Citation numbers in the text and Table 6 do not match the reference list for several studies.",
  "spotCheckPriority": "normal"
 }
}

 "sourceFile": "The Impact of Cold-Water Immersion on Post-Match Recovery in Trained Soccer Players - A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis.pdf",
 "decision": "INCLUDE",
 "exclusionReason": "",

 "doiMissing": false,
 "identityCheck": "Text title 'The Impact of Cold-Water Immersion on Post-Match Recovery in Trained Soccer Players: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis' matches the filename.",
 "confidence": "high",
 "studyDesign": "Systematic Review / Meta-analysis",
 "primaryDomain": "Recovery & Readiness",

 "audiences": ["Performance", "Athletic Training", "Sports Medicine"],
 "sports": ["Soccer"],
 "populations": ["Male Athletes", "Female Athletes", "Mixed / Unspecified"],
 "evidenceSummary": "Systematic review with random-effects meta-analysis of 10 controlled trials in competitive male and female soccer players (aged 15 to 45), comparing cold-water immersion (CWI) with control or placebo after match or simulated match play. CWI improved recovery of maximal voluntary contraction (SMD 1.02, 95% CI 0.55-1.50) and countermovement jump (SMD 0.38, 95% CI 0.12-0.64, evident at 48 h only), reduced creatine kinase (SMD -0.77, 95% CI -1.17 to -0.37) and reduced soreness (SMD -1.04, 95% CI -1.91 to -0.17), with no effect on 20 m sprint (SMD -0.59, 95% CI -1.41 to 0.23).",
 "screeningLimitations": "The included studies were small and blinding of participants and researchers was not possible with CWI, so bias is likely. Every outcome's 95% prediction interval includes a null effect, so the authors advise cautious reading.",
 "synthesisCaution": "Staff could treat CWI as a proven recovery aid for sprint performance or for every post-match outcome, when sprint showed no effect and all prediction intervals include null.",
 "paper": {
  "year": 2026,
  "citation": "Veen J, Bergh C, Cao Y, Randers MB, Krustrup P, Edholm P. The Impact of Cold-Water Immersion on Post-Match Recovery in Trained Soccer Players: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis. Scand J Med Sci Sports. 2026;36:e70202.",
  "doi": "10.1111/sms.70202",
  "abstract": "Systematic review with meta-analysis of 10 controlled trials of cold-water immersion after match or simulated match play in competitive soccer players, measuring sprint, countermovement jump, maximal voluntary contraction, creatine kinase and soreness at 24 to 72 hours.",
  "tldr": "After soccer match play, cold-water immersion improved recovery of maximal strength, reduced creatine kinase and reduced soreness, with a small jump gain at 48 hours. It did not improve sprint recovery, and the prediction intervals are wide enough to include no effect.",
  "methods": "Systematic database search for peer-reviewed controlled trials comparing CWI with control or placebo after match or simulated match play in competitive soccer players, with outcomes at 24, 48 or 72 hours: 20 m sprint, countermovement jump, maximal voluntary contraction, creatine kinase and delayed-onset muscle soreness. Random-effects meta-analysis of standardised mean differences with 95% CIs and prediction intervals; PEDro scale for quality; publication bias assessed qualitatively.",
  "findings": "CWI improved MVC recovery (SMD 1.02) at all time points and CK recovery (SMD -0.77) at all time points. CWI improved CMJ (SMD 0.38), but only at 48 hours. Soreness was reduced at 24 and 72 hours (SMD -1.04). 20 m sprint was unaffected (SMD -0.59, 95% CI -1.41 to 0.23). The prediction intervals for all outcomes included a null effect.",
  "limitations": "Blinding of participants and researchers is impossible with CWI, so bias is possible. The included studies had small samples, which limits statistical power. Publication bias was assessed only qualitatively, and the prediction intervals include null effects.",
  "practicalImplications": "CWI after match play may help soccer players recover strength and reduce soreness and muscle damage markers, but not sprint performance. Because the jump benefit appears only at 48 hours and the prediction intervals are wide, expect modest and variable effects.",
  "athleteDev": "Performance staff can consider CWI as one post-match recovery tool for strength and soreness, not as a sprint-recovery tool. Timing matters, since the jump benefit appeared only at 48 hours.",
  "rtp": "Relevant to recovery after match play in players who are not injured. The review does not study injured players or return-to-play decisions, so it cannot inform clearance or rehabilitation loading."
 }
}

30	  ABSTRACT
31	  Cold-­water immersion (CWI) is widely used by elite soccer players to enhance recovery after match play, yet systematic evidence
32	  supporting the effectiveness of this intervention is lacking. This systematic review with meta-­analysis aimed to evaluate the
33	  effects of CWI on the recovery of physical performance, muscle damage, and delayed muscle soreness in trained soccer players
34	  after match play. A systematic database search was conducted and inclusion criteria were: (1) peer-­reviewed, controlled trials;
35	  (2) competitive soccer players; (3) comparison of CWI with control/placebo after match/simulated match-­play; (4) at least one
36	  of the following outcomes: 20 m sprint, countermovement jump (CMJ), leg strength via maximal voluntary contraction (MVC),
37	  creatine kinase (CK) for muscle damage, or delayed onset of muscle soreness (DOMS); and (5) outcome measurements taken 24,
38	  48 or 72 h post-­match. Random-­effects meta-­analyses were performed to calculate standardized mean differences (SMD) with
39	  95% confidence intervals (CI) and prediction intervals (PI). Ten studies met the inclusion criteria. CWI significantly improved
40	  recovery of MVC (SMD = 1.02 [95% CI: 0.55 to 1.50; 95% PI: −0.48 to 2.53]) and CMJ (SMD = 0.38 [95% CI: 0.12 to 0.64; 95%
41	  PI: −0.39 to 1.15]), while sprint performance remained unaffected (SMD = −0.59 [95% CI: −1.41 to 0.23; 95% PI: −4.14 to 2.95]).
42	  CWI reduced CK levels (SMD = −0.77 [95% CI: −1.17 to −0.37; 95% PI: −2.23 to 0.69]) and alleviated DOMS (SMD = −1.04 [95%
43	  CI: −1.91 to −0.17; 95% PI: −4.12 to 2.03]). MVC and CK recovery improved consistently across all time points, while DOMS relief
44	  was observed at 24 and 72 h post-­match. CMJ benefits were only evident at 48 h post-­match. However, as the 95% PIs for all out-
45	  comes included the null effect, the observed benefits should be interpreted cautiously, as future studies may yield smaller or null
46	  effects. Overall, CWI may enhance recovery of muscle strength, reduce muscle damage, and alleviate soreness in trained male
47	  and female soccer players, but does not seem to impact sprint performance, and its effect on CMJ is time-­dependent.

The Impact of Cold-­Water Immersion on Post-­Match
Recovery in Trained Soccer Players: A Systematic Review
and Meta-­Analysis
Jort Veen1 | Cecilia Bergh2 | Yang Cao2                 | Morten Bredsgaard Randers3               | Peter Krustrup3,4          | Peter Edholm5,6

Correspondence: Peter Edholm (peter.edholm@hh.se)

Received: 26 May 2025 | Revised: 9 October 2025 | Accepted: 20 December 2025

Keywords: cold water immersion | countermovement jump | creatine kinase | DOMS | football | physical performance | recovery


  ABSTRACT
  Cold-­water immersion (CWI) is widely used by elite soccer players to enhance recovery after match play, yet systematic evidence
  supporting the effectiveness of this intervention is lacking. This systematic review with meta-­analysis aimed to evaluate the
  effects of CWI on the recovery of physical performance, muscle damage, and delayed muscle soreness in trained soccer players
  after match play. A systematic database search was conducted and inclusion criteria were: (1) peer-­reviewed, controlled trials;
  (2) competitive soccer players; (3) comparison of CWI with control/placebo after match/simulated match-­play; (4) at least one
  of the following outcomes: 20 m sprint, countermovement jump (CMJ), leg strength via maximal voluntary contraction (MVC),
  creatine kinase (CK) for muscle damage, or delayed onset of muscle soreness (DOMS); and (5) outcome measurements taken 24,
  48 or 72 h post-­match. Random-­effects meta-­analyses were performed to calculate standardized mean differences (SMD) with
  95% confidence intervals (CI) and prediction intervals (PI). Ten studies met the inclusion criteria. CWI significantly improved
  recovery of MVC (SMD = 1.02 [95% CI: 0.55 to 1.50; 95% PI: −0.48 to 2.53]) and CMJ (SMD = 0.38 [95% CI: 0.12 to 0.64; 95%
  PI: −0.39 to 1.15]), while sprint performance remained unaffected (SMD = −0.59 [95% CI: −1.41 to 0.23; 95% PI: −4.14 to 2.95]).
  CWI reduced CK levels (SMD = −0.77 [95% CI: −1.17 to −0.37; 95% PI: −2.23 to 0.69]) and alleviated DOMS (SMD = −1.04 [95%
  CI: −1.91 to −0.17; 95% PI: −4.12 to 2.03]). MVC and CK recovery improved consistently across all time points, while DOMS relief
  was observed at 24 and 72 h post-­match. CMJ benefits were only evident at 48 h post-­match. However, as the 95% PIs for all out-
  comes included the null effect, the observed benefits should be interpreted cautiously, as future studies may yield smaller or null
  effects. Overall, CWI may enhance recovery of muscle strength, reduce muscle damage, and alleviate soreness in trained male
  and female soccer players, but does not seem to impact sprint performance, and its effect on CMJ is time-­dependent.

 "id": "Q19",
 "sourceFile": "The Impact of Cold-Water Immersion on Post-Match Recovery in Trained Soccer Players - A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis.pdf",
 "decision": "INCLUDE",
 "exclusionReason": "",
 "degradedReason": "",
 "doiMissing": false,
 "identityCheck": "Text title 'The Impact of Cold-Water Immersion on Post-Match Recovery in Trained Soccer Players: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis' (Scand J Med Sci Sports 2026; 36:e70202) matches the filename; own DOI 10.1111/sms.70202 is printed on the first page.",
 "confidence": "high",
 "studyDesign": "Systematic Review / Meta-analysis",
 "primaryDomain": "Recovery & Readiness",
 "domains": ["Recovery & Readiness", "Training & Performance"],
 "audiences": ["Performance", "Athletic Training", "Sports Medicine"],
 "sports": ["Soccer"],
 "populations": ["Male Athletes", "Female Athletes", "Mixed / Unspecified"],
 "evidenceSummary": "Systematic review with random-effects meta-analysis of 10 randomized trials (about 210 competitive soccer players by Table 1, only 9 of them female) comparing cold-water immersion (CWI) with passive rest after a match or simulated match. Compared with passive rest, CWI improved recovery of maximal voluntary contraction (SMD 1.02, 95% CI 0.55-1.50) and countermovement jump (SMD 0.38, 95% CI 0.12-0.64, significant at 48 h only), and lowered creatine kinase (SMD -0.77, 95% CI -1.17 to -0.37) and soreness (SMD -1.04, 95% CI -1.91 to -0.17). There was no effect on 20 m sprint (SMD -0.59, 95% CI -1.41 to 0.23).",
 "screeningLimitations": "The trials were small, no trial blinded participants or therapists, and five used simulated rather than real matches. Every outcome's 95% prediction interval includes no effect, and nearly all players were male.",
 "synthesisCaution": "Staff could treat CWI as a proven recovery aid for sprint performance or for every post-match outcome, when sprint showed no effect and all prediction intervals include no effect.",
 "paper": {
  "year": 2026,
  "citation": "Veen J, Bergh C, Cao Y, Randers MB, Krustrup P, Edholm P. The Impact of Cold-Water Immersion on Post-Match Recovery in Trained Soccer Players: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis. Scand J Med Sci Sports. 2026;36:e70202.",
  "doi": "10.1111/sms.70202",
  "abstract": "Systematic review with meta-analysis of 10 controlled trials of cold-water immersion after match or simulated match play in competitive soccer players, measuring sprint, countermovement jump, maximal voluntary contraction, creatine kinase and soreness at 24 to 72 hours. CWI improved strength, jump, creatine kinase and soreness recovery but not sprint, and all prediction intervals included no effect.",
  "tldr": "After soccer match play, cold-water immersion improved recovery of maximal strength, lowered creatine kinase and reduced soreness compared with passive rest, with a small jump gain seen only at 48 hours. It did not improve sprint recovery, and the prediction intervals are wide enough to include no effect.",
  "methods": "PRISMA review (PROSPERO CRD42024543581) searching PubMed, Cochrane, Scopus and SPORTDiscus in January 2024 and January 2025 for RCTs of competitive male or female soccer players aged 15 to 45 given CWI (5-20 min at 5-15 C) or passive or placebo control after a match, simulated match or similar activity. Outcomes were 20 m sprint, countermovement jump, maximal voluntary contraction, creatine kinase and soreness at 24, 48 or 72 h; quality was rated with PEDro and data pooled as SMDs with 95% CIs and prediction intervals (DerSimonian-Laird random effects, Stata 18.5).",
  "findings": "Compared with passive rest, CWI improved MVC recovery overall (SMD 1.02), with effects at 24 h (SMD 1.22), 48 h (SMD 1.10, 95% CI -0.02 to 2.21, p = 0.05) and 72 h (SMD 0.65), and lowered CK at all three time points (overall SMD -0.77). CMJ improved overall (SMD 0.38) but only at 48 h (SMD 0.53), soreness was lower at 24 h and 72 h (overall SMD -1.04) but not at 48 h, and 20 m sprint was unaffected at any time point. The prediction intervals for all outcomes included no effect.",
  "limitations": "Blinding of participants and researchers is impossible with CWI, and no included trial blinded participants or therapists; samples were small (8 to 43 per trial). Publication bias was assessed only qualitatively, the 72 h soreness result rests on one study, and only one trial included female players (9 of 22). The 48 h MVC effect is called significant although its 95% CI crosses zero.",
  "practicalImplications": "Post-match CWI (8-15 C for 5-15 min in these trials) may help soccer players recover strength and reduce soreness and creatine kinase over the next three days. It showed no sprint benefit, and the wide prediction intervals mean the effect in a given team may be small or absent.",
  "athleteDev": "Performance staff can consider CWI as one post-match recovery tool for strength and soreness, not as a sprint-recovery tool. The jump benefit appeared only at the 48 h test, so a jump test the day after a match may not show it.",
  "rtp": "Relevant to recovery after match play in players who are not injured. The review does not study injured players or return-to-play decisions, so it cannot inform clearance or rehabilitation loading."
 },
 "verification": {
  "status": "CORRECTED",
  "changes": [
   "evidenceSummary: 'competitive male and female soccer players (aged 15 to 45)' -> about 210 players by Table 1, only 9 female; 15 to 45 is the inclusion criterion, not the sample (Rupp et al. '13 males, 9 females', all others males)",
   "evidenceSummary: 'compared with control or placebo' -> passive rest, the comparator the results report ('compared to passive rest')",
   "screeningLimitations: added no participant or therapist blinding in any trial ('In none of the included studies were participants and/or therapists blinded') and simulated match protocols",
   "paper.findings: added time-point SMDs and that the 48 h MVC CI crosses zero ('SMD = 1.10 [95% CI: -0.02 to 2.21]'); soreness not reduced at 48 h",
   "paper.methods: added databases, search dates, PROSPERO ID, CWI protocol criteria and analysis model",
   "paper.limitations: added single-study 72 h soreness result, one trial with 9 females, and trial size range",
   "paper.athleteDev: 'Timing matters, since the jump benefit appeared only at 48 hours' (implied CWI timing) -> the benefit was seen only at the 48 h test"
  ],
  "residualConcerns": "The total sample is not stated in the text; about 210 is the sum of Table 1. The paper reports that studies were included only with a PEDro score of 5 or more and calls this low risk of bias, although no trial was blinded.",
  "spotCheckPriority": "normal"
 }
}

16	  Abstract
17	  Background Creatine monohydrate is a widely used dietary supplement with proven benefits in athletic
18	  performance and potential therapeutic applications in clinical populations. However, concerns regarding its impact
19	  on renal function persist, largely due to elevated serum creatinine levels associated with creatine intake.
20	  Methods A comprehensive literature search was conducted in PubMed, Scopus, Web of Science, and Google
21	  Scholar for studies published between January 2000 and March 2025. Primary outcomes were serum creatinine and
22	  glomerular filtration rate (GFR). Meta-analyses were performed using a random-effects model, with subgroup analysis
23	  by supplementation duration.
24	  Results Twenty-one studies were included in the systematic review, and 12 studies (177 participants in the creatine
25	  group and 263 in control) were eligible for meta-analysis of serum creatinine levels. Creatine supplementation was
26	  associated with a small but statistically significant increase in serum creatinine (MD: 0.07 µmol/L; 95% CI: 0.01 to 0.12;
27	  p = 0.03). Subgroup analysis of the creatinine outcome based on follow-up duration revealed that the intervention
28	  effect was significant in studies with a follow-up of ≤ 1 week (MD = 0.12; 95% CI: 0.03 to 0.21). However, no significant
29	  effect was observed in studies with a follow-up of 1 to 12 weeks (MD = 0.04; 95% CI: − 0.09 to 0.17). The effect became
30	  significant again in studies with a follow-up of more than 12 weeks. The meta-analysis revealed a non-statistically
31	  significant differences in GFR following creatine supplementation compared to control.
32	  Conclusion Creatine supplementation is associated with a modest, transient increase in serum creatinine levels,
33	  likely due to metabolic turnover rather than renal impairment. No significant changes were observed in GFR,
34	  suggesting preserved kidney function.
35	  Clinical trial number Not applicable.

Effect of creatine supplementation on kidney
function: a systematic review and meta-
analysis
Elham Kabiri Naeini1, Milad Eskandari1*, Mojgan Mortazavi1, Alieh Gholaminejad2 and Negar Karevan3


  Abstract
  Background Creatine monohydrate is a widely used dietary supplement with proven benefits in athletic
  performance and potential therapeutic applications in clinical populations. However, concerns regarding its impact
  on renal function persist, largely due to elevated serum creatinine levels associated with creatine intake.
  Methods A comprehensive literature search was conducted in PubMed, Scopus, Web of Science, and Google
  Scholar for studies published between January 2000 and March 2025. Primary outcomes were serum creatinine and
  glomerular filtration rate (GFR). Meta-analyses were performed using a random-effects model, with subgroup analysis
  by supplementation duration.
  Results Twenty-one studies were included in the systematic review, and 12 studies (177 participants in the creatine
  group and 263 in control) were eligible for meta-analysis of serum creatinine levels. Creatine supplementation was
  associated with a small but statistically significant increase in serum creatinine (MD: 0.07 µmol/L; 95% CI: 0.01 to 0.12;
  p = 0.03). Subgroup analysis of the creatinine outcome based on follow-up duration revealed that the intervention
  effect was significant in studies with a follow-up of ≤ 1 week (MD = 0.12; 95% CI: 0.03 to 0.21). However, no significant
  effect was observed in studies with a follow-up of 1 to 12 weeks (MD = 0.04; 95% CI: − 0.09 to 0.17). The effect became
  significant again in studies with a follow-up of more than 12 weeks. The meta-analysis revealed a non-statistically
  significant differences in GFR following creatine supplementation compared to control.
  Conclusion Creatine supplementation is associated with a modest, transient increase in serum creatinine levels,
  likely due to metabolic turnover rather than renal impairment. No significant changes were observed in GFR,
  suggesting preserved kidney function.
  Clinical trial number Not applicable.
  Keywords Creatine supplementation, Kidney function, Serum creatinine, Glomerular filtration rate, Renal safety,
  Meta-analysis

Conclusion
In summary, this systematic review and meta-analysis
demonstrate that creatine supplementation is associ-
ated with a modest increase in serum creatinine levels
but does not adversely affect glomerular filtration rate.
These results indicate that creatine is likely safe for kid-
ney function in healthy individuals and various clinical
populations when used within standard dosing protocols.
However, researchers and clinicians should interpret
elevated serum creatinine levels in the context of supple-
mentation with caution and consider more specific renal
function markers for accurate assessment.

19	  Abstract
20	  Background Muscle lesions are common sport injuries resulting in prolonged absence from sport activity and long
21	  rehabilitation periods. The aim of this systematic review and meta-analysis was to quantify the clinical benefits of
22	  platelet-rich plasma (PRP) injections in treating acute muscle injuries.
23	  Methods The search was conducted on PubMed, Cochrane Library, and Web of Science in January 2026. The PRISMA
24	  guidelines were used. Inclusion criteria were: randomized controlled trials (RCTs) published in English comparing
25	  PRP injections with control (rehabilitation or placebo) for the treatment of acute muscle injuries. The outcomes
26	  analysed were: time to return to sport (RTS), Visual Analogue Scale (VAS) for pain, re-injury and complication rates.
27	  Two sub-analyses were performed, one on the double-blind RCTs and one on the RCTs focusing on hamstrings. A
28	  fragility analysis was performed using the fragility index (FI) and the continuous FI (CFI). The quality of each article was
29	  assessed using the Cochrane RoB 2 and the GRADE tools.
30	  Results Among the 4969 articles retrieved, nine RCTs (474 patients) were included. PRP provided faster RTS both in
31	  the overall analysis (p < 0.001, mean difference (MD) = 7.5, CFI = 188) and in the two sub-analyses (p < 0.001, MD = 8.8,
32	  CFI = 67 and p = 0.001, MD = 7.5, CFI = 97 respectively), as well as superior VAS improvement in the hamstring sub-
33	  analysis (p = 0.006, MD = 0.4, CFI = 22). No difference was found in terms of re-injury and complication rates between
34	  the two groups (FI = 5 and FI = 7, respectively). The evaluation using the RoB 2 tool showed that four studies had a
35	  “low risk” of bias and five had a “high risk” of bias. The GRADE evaluation showed a limited quality of evidence of the
36	  analysed outcomes.
37	  Conclusion PRP produced a faster RTS compared to controls in acute muscle injury patients, both in the overall
38	  analysis and in the sub-analyses. PRP was able to produce a statistically higher pain relief only in the hamstring

Platelet-Rich Plasma Accelerates the Return
to Sport in Athletes with Acute Muscle
Injuries: A Systematic Review and Statistical
Fragility Index-Based Meta-Analysis
of Randomized Controlled Trials
Alessandro Bensa1,2* , Gae Fattini Fellini1, Angelo Boffa3, Alberto Grassi4, Kristian Samuelsson5 and
Giuseppe Filardo1,2


  Abstract
  Background Muscle lesions are common sport injuries resulting in prolonged absence from sport activity and long
  rehabilitation periods. The aim of this systematic review and meta-analysis was to quantify the clinical benefits of
  platelet-rich plasma (PRP) injections in treating acute muscle injuries.
  Methods The search was conducted on PubMed, Cochrane Library, and Web of Science in January 2026. The PRISMA
  guidelines were used. Inclusion criteria were: randomized controlled trials (RCTs) published in English comparing
  PRP injections with control (rehabilitation or placebo) for the treatment of acute muscle injuries. The outcomes
  analysed were: time to return to sport (RTS), Visual Analogue Scale (VAS) for pain, re-injury and complication rates.
  Two sub-analyses were performed, one on the double-blind RCTs and one on the RCTs focusing on hamstrings. A
  fragility analysis was performed using the fragility index (FI) and the continuous FI (CFI). The quality of each article was
  assessed using the Cochrane RoB 2 and the GRADE tools.
  Results Among the 4969 articles retrieved, nine RCTs (474 patients) were included. PRP provided faster RTS both in
  the overall analysis (p < 0.001, mean difference (MD) = 7.5, CFI = 188) and in the two sub-analyses (p < 0.001, MD = 8.8,
  CFI = 67 and p = 0.001, MD = 7.5, CFI = 97 respectively), as well as superior VAS improvement in the hamstring sub-
  analysis (p = 0.006, MD = 0.4, CFI = 22). No difference was found in terms of re-injury and complication rates between
  the two groups (FI = 5 and FI = 7, respectively). The evaluation using the RoB 2 tool showed that four studies had a
  “low risk” of bias and five had a “high risk” of bias. The GRADE evaluation showed a limited quality of evidence of the
  analysed outcomes.
  Conclusion PRP produced a faster RTS compared to controls in acute muscle injury patients, both in the overall
  analysis and in the sub-analyses. PRP was able to produce a statistically higher pain relief only in the hamstring

15	  Abstract
16	  Background Ankle syndesmosis injuries are a significant concern in elite athletes, often resulting in prolonged
17	  recovery and uncertainty regarding optimal management. Although most athletes eventually return to sport (RTS),
18	  reported RTS rates and timelines vary widely due to differences in treatment strategies. Given this heterogeneity and
19	  lack of consensus, this study systematically reviews RTS rates and time to RTS in elite athletes following syndesmotic
20	  ankle injuries.
21	  Methods A systematic search of five databases was performed through September 2025 to identify studies on RTS
22	  outcomes in elite athletes with ankle syndesmosis injuries. Pooled RTS proportions were calculated using a random-
23	  effects model with logit transformation, and time outcomes were synthesized using random-effects models or
24	  descriptive methods. Subgroup, sensitivity, and meta-regression analyses were conducted to assess heterogeneity.
25	  Study quality was evaluated using the Newcastle–Ottawa Scale, and publication bias was assessed with funnel plots
26	  and Egger’s test.
27	  Results Fourteen studies comprising 901 elite athletes were included. The pooled RTS rate following ankle
28	  syndesmosis injuries was 96% (95% CI 93–98%), with low-to-moderate heterogeneity (I2 = 27%). Subgroup analysis
29	  showed comparable RTS rates for suture-button fixation (98%) and nonoperative management (98%). Sensitivity
30	  analyses confirmed the robustness of the findings. Publication bias was suggested by funnel plot asymmetry and
31	  Egger’s test (p = 0.0002). The average time to RTS across studies was approximately 58 days.
32	  Conclusion Elite athletes sustaining ankle syndesmosis injuries demonstrate a high likelihood of returning to
33	  sport, with a pooled RTS rate of 96%. Comparable outcomes were observed following both suture-button fixation
34	  and nonoperative management, with most athletes resuming play within 2 months. Most athletes can anticipate
35	  favorable outcomes regardless of treatment strategy, though management should still be individualized based on
36	  injury severity and sport-specific demands.
37	  Keywords Ankle syndesmosis injury, High ankle sprain, Elite athletes, Return to sport, Rehabilitation

Return-to-sport rate and time in elite athletes
after ankle syndesmosis injuries: a systematic
review and meta-analysis
Ran Li1, Changlu Sun2, Pengkun Qi3* and Zhonghao Xu2*


  Abstract
  Background Ankle syndesmosis injuries are a significant concern in elite athletes, often resulting in prolonged
  recovery and uncertainty regarding optimal management. Although most athletes eventually return to sport (RTS),
  reported RTS rates and timelines vary widely due to differences in treatment strategies. Given this heterogeneity and
  lack of consensus, this study systematically reviews RTS rates and time to RTS in elite athletes following syndesmotic
  ankle injuries.
  Methods A systematic search of five databases was performed through September 2025 to identify studies on RTS
  outcomes in elite athletes with ankle syndesmosis injuries. Pooled RTS proportions were calculated using a random-
  effects model with logit transformation, and time outcomes were synthesized using random-effects models or
  descriptive methods. Subgroup, sensitivity, and meta-regression analyses were conducted to assess heterogeneity.
  Study quality was evaluated using the Newcastle–Ottawa Scale, and publication bias was assessed with funnel plots
  and Egger’s test.
  Results Fourteen studies comprising 901 elite athletes were included. The pooled RTS rate following ankle
  syndesmosis injuries was 96% (95% CI 93–98%), with low-to-moderate heterogeneity (I2 = 27%). Subgroup analysis
  showed comparable RTS rates for suture-button fixation (98%) and nonoperative management (98%). Sensitivity
  analyses confirmed the robustness of the findings. Publication bias was suggested by funnel plot asymmetry and
  Egger’s test (p = 0.0002). The average time to RTS across studies was approximately 58 days.
  Conclusion Elite athletes sustaining ankle syndesmosis injuries demonstrate a high likelihood of returning to
  sport, with a pooled RTS rate of 96%. Comparable outcomes were observed following both suture-button fixation
  and nonoperative management, with most athletes resuming play within 2 months. Most athletes can anticipate
  favorable outcomes regardless of treatment strategy, though management should still be individualized based on
  injury severity and sport-specific demands.
  Keywords Ankle syndesmosis injury, High ankle sprain, Elite athletes, Return to sport, Rehabilitation

 "sourceFile": "Return-to-sport rate and time in elite athletes after ankle syndesmosis injuries - a systematic review and meta-analysis.pdf",

 "confidence": "high",
 "studyDesign": "Systematic Review / Meta-analysis",
 "primaryDomain": "Rehabilitation & Return to Sport",
 "domains": ["Rehabilitation & Return to Sport", "Sports Medicine & Injury"],
 "audiences": ["Sports Medicine", "Rehabilitation", "Athletic Training"],
 "sports": ["American Football", "Soccer", "Rugby", "Ice Hockey", "Mixed / General Sport"],
 "populations": ["Professional / Elite", "Collegiate", "Injured Athletes"],
 "evidenceSummary": "Systematic review and meta-analysis of 14 mostly observational studies (901 professional and collegiate athletes, mean age 26.8) with ankle syndesmosis injuries, pooling return-to-sport rates with logit-transformed random-effects models. The pooled rate of return to match play was 96% (95% CI 93-98%; I2 27%), 98% after suture-button fixation and 98% after nonoperative management. Time to return was only averaged across studies (unweighted, about 58 days, range 13-133).",
 "screeningLimitations": "Thirteen of 14 studies reported 100% return, the only lower rate came from the largest NFL cohort (478 of 533, 89.7%), and Egger's test suggested publication bias (p = 0.0002). GRADE certainty was low for return rate and very low for return time, which was not pooled.",
 "synthesisCaution": "Staff could plan on 'about two months' for any syndesmosis injury, when that figure is an unweighted average that mixes stable injuries managed nonoperatively (about 13 to 45 days) with high-grade injuries fixed with suture-button (about 41 to 133 days).",
 "paper": {
  "year": 2026,
  "citation": "Li R, Sun C, Qi P, Xu Z. Return-to-sport rate and time in elite athletes after ankle syndesmosis injuries: a systematic review and meta-analysis. J Orthop Surg Res. 2026;21:69.",
  "doi": "10.1186/s13018-025-06566-6",
  "abstract": "Systematic review and meta-analysis of 14 studies (901 elite athletes) with ankle syndesmosis injuries, pooling return-to-sport rate and summarising time to return. Pooled return to match play was 96%, with similar rates after suture-button fixation and nonoperative management, and time to return averaged about 58 days across studies.",
  "tldr": "Almost all professional and collegiate athletes in these studies returned to match play after an ankle syndesmosis injury (pooled 96%). Return time depended heavily on severity and treatment, from about two weeks for stable sprains managed without surgery to three or four months after surgical fixation.",
  "methods": "PRISMA review (PROSPERO CRD420251149156) searching PubMed, Embase, Web of Science and the Cochrane Library to September 2025 for cohort studies, RCTs and case series reporting return to sport in elite or professional athletes with syndesmosis injury. Return rates were pooled with logit-transformed random-effects models in R, with subgroup, leave-one-out and meta-regression analyses; quality was rated with the Newcastle-Ottawa Scale, certainty with GRADE, and publication bias with funnel plots and Egger's test.",
  "findings": "Pooled return to match play was 96% (95% CI 93-98%), 98% for suture-button fixation (95% CI 92-99%) and 98% for nonoperative management (95% CI 94-99%), with 90% (95% CI 83-95%) in studies not reporting treatment (subgroup difference p = 0.014). Leaving out the large NFL cohort raised the pooled rate to 98% with no heterogeneity. Time to return, reported in 13 studies, averaged about 58 days unweighted (range 13-133), with Table 1 showing roughly 13 to 45 days in nonoperative studies and 41 to 133 days in suture-button studies.",
  "limitations": "Studies were mostly retrospective and observational with limited control of confounding, and publication bias suggests the pooled rate may be overestimated. Time to return lacked variability measures, so the 58-day figure is an unweighted descriptive average with limited inferential value. Treatment groups differ in injury grade (stable injuries treated nonoperatively, unstable injuries fixed), so similar return rates do not show the treatments are interchangeable; the abstract says five databases while the methods list four.",
  "practicalImplications": "Athletes with a syndesmosis injury can be told that return to match play is very likely, but the expected timeline should be set by injury grade and treatment rather than a single average. In these studies stable, low-grade injuries managed nonoperatively returned in weeks, while high-grade injuries needing fixation took about two to four months.",
  "athleteDev": "Limited direct use for performance staff beyond planning: the review reports whether and roughly when athletes returned, not performance after return or the rehabilitation content. Use the severity- and treatment-specific ranges from the study table, not the overall 58-day average, when planning an athlete's absence.",
  "rtp": "Relevant to expectation setting after syndesmosis injury in professional and collegiate athletes: nearly all returned to match play. It cannot set clearance criteria or an individual timeline, because return time was not pooled and return to pre-injury performance level was not assessed."
 },
 "verification": {
  "status": "CORRECTED",
  "changes": [
   "sports: added Soccer (D'Hooghe, Qatar 'professional football players', described in the discussion as 'professional soccer players') and Mixed / General Sport (Calde, Taylor, Nussbaum, Altmeppen list 'athletes' or 'college athletes'); kept American Football (NFL and collegiate football), Rugby and Ice Hockey from Table 1",
   "populations: added Collegiate (Miller 'collegiate football players', Taylor and Nussbaum 'college athletes')",
   "screeningLimitations and synthesisCaution: added that 13 of 14 studies reported 100% return and only the NFL cohort (478/533) was lower, GRADE low/very low, and that the 58-day figure mixes nonoperative and surgical cases",
   "paper.findings: added subgroup CIs, the 90% rate in treatment-not-reported studies (p = 0.0136), the leave-one-out result and the treatment-specific time ranges from Table 1",
   "paper.tldr, practicalImplications, athleteDev: 'roughly two-month timeline as planning benchmarks' -> timeline set by injury grade and treatment (nonoperative about 13-45 days, suture-button 41-133 days in Table 1)",
   "paper.limitations: added confounding by injury grade between treatment groups and the five-versus-four database discrepancy",
   "paper.methods: listed databases, PROSPERO ID, designs and GRADE"
  ],
  "residualConcerns": "The treatment-specific time ranges are read from Table 1, not pooled by the authors. Table 1 lists 'hockey players' without saying ice hockey (Canadian and US professional cohorts), and Sikka et al. is described with an 'anterior talofibular ligament' injury, a lateral ligament, which may be a table error. Sex was not reported, so no sex tags were added. Return-to-sport topic, so clinically sensitive.",
  "spotCheckPriority": "high"
 }
}

                                                                                  We conducted sensitivity analyses to assess the robustness

                                                                             model (MD = 0.02 ◦ C/min, 95% CI: 0.01–0.03, p < 0.00001). In
                                                                             subgroup analyses, excluding Hosokawa Y’s (2020) study form the

                                                                                  Publication bias was assessed using funnel plots and Egger’s
                                                                             test because the primary outcome included ≥10 studies (Figure 7).
                                                                             Visual asymmetry in funnel plots and a signiﬁcant Egger’s test
                                                                             (t = 3.40, p = 0.005) suggested potential publication bias or
                                                                             small-study eﬀects. Although high heterogeneity (I² = 88%) may
                                                                             contribute to funnel plot asymmetry, the signiﬁcant Egger’s test
                                                                             indicates that the distribution of eﬀect sizes is not fully explained
                                                                             by heterogeneity alone. This suggests that negative or null results
                                                                             may be under-represented in small studies, potentially inﬂating
                                                                             the eﬀect estimates for portable active cooling interventions. This
                                                                             potential bias warrants careful consideration when interpreting and
                                                                             generalizing the meta-analytic results.

                                                                                Beyond these practical considerations, the lack of signiﬁcant
                                                                            diﬀerence in cooling eﬃcacy between type B devices and
                                                                            passive cooling can be attributed to multiple thermodynamic,
                                                                            physiological, and design limitations. First, type B devices depend
                                                                            on a ﬁnite cold storage capacity; phase-change materials or
                                                                            chemical refrigerants rapidly reach thermal saturation under high
                                                                            ambient temperatures, failing to sustain the cooling required
                                                                            during the “golden 30-min” window (43). Second, these vests
                                                                            primarily cover the anterior and posterior torso, an area
                                                                            with limited total heat exchange capacity (44, 45). A deeper
                                                                            physiological explanation lies in the fundamental diﬀerences
                                                                            in thermal exchange between glabrous (hairless) and non-
                                                                            glabrous skin. Glabrous skin surfaces—the palms, soles, face,
                                                                            and ears—constitute only a small percentage of total body
                                                                            surface area but contain specialized vascular structures called
                                                                            arteriovenous anastomoses (AVAs). These direct connections

546	
547	                                                                                  We conducted sensitivity analyses to assess the robustness
548	                                                                             of the primary outcome ﬁndings. Leave-one-out showed that no
549	                                                                             single study dispriportionately inﬂuenced the pooled eﬀect; the MD
550	                                                                             ranged from 0.01 to 0.03 ◦ C/min, and all p < 0.05. A ﬁxed-eﬀects
551	                                                                             model producted similar results (MD = 0.01 ◦ C/min, 95% CI:
552	                                                                             0.01–0.01, p < 0.00001) compared with the primary random-eﬀects
553	                                                                             model (MD = 0.02 ◦ C/min, 95% CI: 0.01–0.03, p < 0.00001). In
554	                                                                             subgroup analyses, excluding Hosokawa Y’s (2020) study form the
555	                                                                             type B device analysis reduced heterogeneity from 45 to 0% without
556	                                                                             materially altering the MD, CI, or p-value.
557	                                                                                  Publication bias was assessed using funnel plots and Egger’s
558	                                                                             test because the primary outcome included ≥10 studies (Figure 7).
559	                                                                             Visual asymmetry in funnel plots and a signiﬁcant Egger’s test
560	                                                                             (t = 3.40, p = 0.005) suggested potential publication bias or
561	                                                                             small-study eﬀects. Although high heterogeneity (I² = 88%) may
562	                                                                             contribute to funnel plot asymmetry, the signiﬁcant Egger’s test
563	                                                                             indicates that the distribution of eﬀect sizes is not fully explained
564	                                                                             by heterogeneity alone. This suggests that negative or null results
565	                                                                             may be under-represented in small studies, potentially inﬂating
566	                                                                             the eﬀect estimates for portable active cooling interventions. This
567	                                                                             potential bias warrants careful consideration when interpreting and
568	                                                                             generalizing the meta-analytic results.

I checked all seven records and wrote them to /Users/kristinarash/.claude/jobs/219ddd5b/tmp/batch133/verified/Q17.json through Q23.json. Each one parses with json.tool, uses only taxonomy values and has no em dashes. Each paper's own DOI is printed in its header, so none was marked missing. I read each text through to the references; nothing sits after the reference lists.

Q17 | CORRECTED | INCLUDE | high | the -0.38 vertical-jump sign is negative everywhere it's printed (abstract, results text, Table 7) and is never explained, so I flagged it as unresolved; added Egger publication bias with a trim-and-fill CI that crosses zero, the table-vs-text mismatches, and softened "prioritise resisted sprint training" (no overall sprint advantage over unresisted, p = 0.057); added Track & Field, Tennis, Other Sport and Female Athletes
Q18 | CORRECTED | INCLUDE | high | GRADE was very low for every outcome, not "mixed"; the findings were thin, so I added the single-study associations with their sample sizes (8 to 16 sprinters) and the many null results; the paper contradicts itself on the direction of the Trivers knee-width result; added Professional / Elite and Youth / Adolescent
Q19 | CORRECTED | INCLUDE | normal | "aged 15 to 45" was the inclusion criterion, not the sample (about 210 players by Table 1, only 9 female); the comparator is passive rest; no trial was blinded; the 48 h strength CI crosses zero; fixed athleteDev's wording that implied CWI timing matters
Q20 | DECISION_CHANGED | INCLUDE | high | changed EXCLUDE (c) to INCLUDE under the library precedent: creatine kidney safety is an athlete-health question, the paper is framed around athletes, and it includes American football and trained samples; I filled every field and used no athlete tags; flagged the 0.07 µmol/L unit, the conflicting study counts (12/14/16) and that no pooled GFR estimate is printed
Q21 | CORRECTED | INCLUDE | high | dropped Injured Athletes and Soccer because the body describes "patients" and soccer appears only in a reference title (residualConcerns notes the counter-argument); fixed the synthesisCaution that read the fragility index of 188 as a weakness when it indicates robustness; added I2 92%, five high-risk-of-bias trials, the mix of comparators, and the discussion's wrong claim about the double-blind pain result
Q22 | CORRECTED | INCLUDE | high | rebuilt sports and population tags from Table 1 (added Soccer, Mixed / General Sport and Collegiate); the "about 58 days" is an unweighted average that mixes nonoperative cases (about 13-45 days) with suture-button fixation (41-133 days); 13 of 14 studies reported 100% return, and only the large NFL cohort was lower
Q23 | CORRECTED | INCLUDE | high | removed every implication of clinical heat stroke evidence: participants were healthy volunteers with exercise-induced hyperthermia, and cold-water immersion remains the gold standard; changed population tags to Adult / Recreational and removed Soccer; corrected the type A CI to the results value (0.02-0.07; the abstract prints 0.02-0.04); the type A advantage comes mainly from ice-water tarp cooling; added I2 88% and Egger p = 0.005

Two things a reviewer should look at:
- **Q20 decision:** this is a judgement call under rule (c), and the reasoning is in residualConcerns. Two items there are my own inference and are not stated in the text: that the creatinine unit is probably mg/dL, and that the American Football tag rests on "Football Players" in two US studies.
- **Q17 jump result:** the direction of the vertical-jump effect cannot be confirmed from the text.

I wrote no scratch files.
